title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
similar_questions: 698. Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets
1981. Minimize the Difference Between Target and Chosen Elements

scenarios.description: Distributing computational tasks across two servers to achieve equal workload, ensuring optimal resource utilization and performance.
Fairly dividing a set of assets between two heirs such that each receives assets of equal total value.
Splitting players with different skill levels into two teams with equal total skill points to ensure a fair match.

solutions.title: Recursion
solutions.approach: Use recursive backtracking to try all possible ways of selecting elements. For each element, we have two choices: include it in the current subset or exclude it. Check if we can form a subset with sum equal to half of the total sum.
solutions.explanation: The recursive solution first checks if the total sum is odd - if so, we cannot partition into equal subsets. Then it calculates the target sum (total/2). For each element starting from index 0, we try two options: skip the element (move to next index with same target) or include it (move to next index with reduced target). The base case is when we've processed all elements - we return true if target is exactly 0, meaning we found a valid subset. If target becomes negative, we return false as we've exceeded the target. This explores all 2^n possible subsets.

complexity_explanation.time: At each position, we make two recursive calls (include or exclude), creating a binary tree of depth n. This results in exploring up to 2^n possible subsets in the worst case.
complexity_explanation.space: The recursion stack can go as deep as n levels (when processing all elements), requiring O(n) space for the call stack.

solutions.why_it_works: This solution works by systematically exploring all possible ways to select elements that sum to the target. The key insight is that if we can find any subset with sum equal to total/2, then the remaining elements must also sum to total/2 (since total - total/2 = total/2). We use backtracking to try both including and excluding each element. The base cases handle when we've processed all elements (check if target is 0) and when we've exceeded the target (return false). While correct, this exponential solution is inefficient due to solving the same subproblems repeatedly.

solutions.title: Dynamic Programming (Top-Down)
solutions.approach: Add 2D memoization to the recursive solution. Store results for each (index, target) pair to avoid recomputing the same subproblems. This transforms the exponential solution into polynomial time.
solutions.explanation: This solution optimizes the recursive approach by adding memoization. We create a 2D memo array where memo[i][target] stores whether we can achieve the target sum using elements from index i onward. Before computing dfs(i, target), we check if it's already in memo. If so, return the cached result. Otherwise, compute it using the same logic as recursion: try excluding (dfs(i+1, target)) or including (dfs(i+1, target-nums[i])) the current element. Store the result in memo before returning. Base cases check if target is 0 (success) or if we've run out of elements or target is negative (failure). This eliminates redundant computations.

complexity_explanation.time: There are n possible indices and target+1 possible target values, giving n*(target+1) unique states. Each state is computed once due to memoization, and each computation does O(1) work. Total time is O(n*target).

solutions.why_it_works: Memoization eliminates exponential time by caching results for each unique (index, target) state. The key observation is that whether we can achieve a target sum from index i onwards depends only on i and target, not on the path taken to reach this state. This creates overlapping subproblems - the same (i, target) pair can be reached through different element selection paths. By storing the result the first time we compute each state, all subsequent lookups are O(1). This preserves correctness while achieving polynomial time complexity. The memo table effectively builds a solution bottom-up as recursion unwinds.

solutions.title: Dynamic Programming (Bottom-Up)
solutions.approach: Build a 2D DP table iteratively where dp[i][j] represents whether we can achieve sum j using the first i elements. Fill the table row by row, and the answer is in dp[n][target].
solutions.explanation: The bottom-up approach builds the solution iteratively without recursion. We create a 2D boolean table dp where dp[i][j] indicates whether we can achieve sum j using the first i elements from nums. We initialize the base case: dp[i][0] = True for all i (we can always achieve sum 0 by selecting nothing). Then we iterate through each element (i from 1 to n) and each possible sum (j from 1 to target). For each cell, if the current element nums[i-1] is <= j, we can either exclude it (dp[i-1][j]) or include it (dp[i-1][j-nums[i-1]]). Otherwise, we can only exclude it. The answer is dp[n][target]. This builds solutions from smaller subproblems to larger ones.

solutions.why_it_works: Bottom-up DP builds solutions iteratively from base cases. The recurrence relation is: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] (exclude nums[i-1]) OR dp[i-1][j-nums[i-1]] (include nums[i-1], if possible). By filling the table row by row (for each element) and column by column (for each sum), we ensure that when computing dp[i][j], all values dp[i-1][*] have already been computed. The base case dp[*][0] = True (empty subset sums to 0) provides the foundation. This eliminates recursion overhead while maintaining the same time complexity as top-down. The table provides a clear visualization of which sums are achievable at each step.

solutions.title: Dynamic Programming (Space Optimized)
solutions.approach: Optimize the 2D DP by observing that we only need the previous row to compute the current row. Use two 1D arrays that alternate roles, reducing space complexity from O(n*target) to O(target).
solutions.explanation: This solution optimizes space by noticing that dp[i][j] only depends on dp[i-1][j] and dp[i-1][j-nums[i-1]], meaning we only need the previous row. We maintain two 1D arrays: dp (previous row) and nextDp (current row being computed). We initialize dp[0] = True (base case). For each element, we compute nextDp based on dp: for each sum j, if j >= nums[i], nextDp[j] = dp[j] OR dp[j-nums[i]]; otherwise nextDp[j] = dp[j]. After processing all sums for an element, we swap dp and nextDp. The answer is dp[target]. This reduces space from O(n*target) to O(target) while maintaining the same time complexity.

solutions.why_it_works: This optimization works because each row in the 2D DP table depends only on the previous row, not on any earlier rows. By maintaining just two arrays (current and previous), we can compute the same values. The swap operation makes the current row become the previous row for the next iteration. This preserves correctness because we never need to look back more than one row. The trade-off is slightly more complex code (managing two arrays and swapping) for significant space savings, especially when n is large.

solutions.title: Dynamic Programming (Hash Set)
solutions.approach: Use a hash set to track all achievable sums instead of a boolean array. For each element, create a new set containing all previous sums plus sums obtained by adding the current element. Check if target sum is ever achieved.
solutions.explanation: This solution uses a set-based approach instead of arrays. We maintain a set dp containing all currently achievable sums, initialized with {0}. For each element (iterating backward for clarity), we create a new set nextDP. For each sum t in dp, we add both t (exclude current element) and t+nums[i] (include current element) to nextDP. As an optimization, if t+nums[i] equals target, we immediately return true. Otherwise, we update dp = nextDP and continue. If we process all elements without finding target, return false. This approach naturally handles sparse sums and can be more intuitive than arrays.

solutions.title: Dynamic Programming (Optimal)
solutions.approach: Use a single 1D boolean array and iterate backward through possible sums for each element. This eliminates the need for two arrays while maintaining correctness. This is the most space-efficient standard DP approach.
solutions.explanation: This is the optimal standard DP solution. We use a single 1D array dp where dp[j] indicates whether sum j is achievable. The key insight is that by iterating backward through sums (from target down to nums[i]), we avoid overwriting values we still need to read in the same iteration. For each element nums[i], we iterate j from target down to nums[i]. For each j, we update dp[j] = dp[j] OR dp[j-nums[i]]. The backward iteration ensures that when we read dp[j-nums[i]], it still contains the value from the previous element (before including nums[i]), not a value that includes nums[i] multiple times. This is the most elegant and commonly used solution.

solutions.why_it_works: The critical insight is the backward iteration. When we process element nums[i], we update dp[j] based on dp[j-nums[i]]. If we iterated forward, we might update dp[j-nums[i]] first, then incorrectly use this updated value when computing dp[j], effectively using nums[i] multiple times. By iterating backward, when we compute dp[j], the value dp[j-nums[i]] still represents achievability without nums[i] (or with previous elements only), ensuring each element is used at most once. This preserves the 0/1 knapsack property. The OR operation combines the exclude (dp[j]) and include (dp[j-num]) cases.

pro_tips: This is the most elegant and commonly used solution - memorize this pattern for 0/1 knapsack problems.

solutions.title: Dynamic Programming (Bitset)
solutions.approach: Use bit manipulation to represent the DP state. Each bit position represents whether that sum is achievable. Use bitwise OR and left shift operations to efficiently update the state for each element. This is a low-level optimization for competitive programming.
solutions.explanation: This advanced solution uses bitwise operations for ultimate efficiency. We represent the DP state as a single integer (bitset) where bit i is 1 if sum i is achievable, 0 otherwise. We initialize with dp = 1 (bit 0 set, representing sum 0). For each element num, we compute dp |= (dp << num), which means: shift dp left by num positions (creating new achievable sums by adding num to all previous sums) and OR with original dp (preserving exclude case). After processing all elements, we check if bit at position target is set using (dp & (1 << target)) != 0. This uses bitwise operations to parallelize the DP updates, though in practice it's mainly a space optimization and coding challenge.

complexity_explanation.time: For each of n elements, we perform a left shift operation (O(target/w) where w is word size, typically constant) and an OR operation. In practice, this is O(n*target) with very low constant factors due to bitwise operations being hardware-optimized.
complexity_explanation.space: The bitset requires target+1 bits, which is approximately target/8 bytes (or target/64 64-bit words). This is O(target) in bit space, more compact than boolean arrays.

solutions.why_it_works: This solution encodes the entire DP state in a single bitset. The operation dp |= (dp << num) is equivalent to the standard DP update: for each achievable sum j (represented by bit j being 1), we can now also achieve sum j+num (by shifting). The OR operation combines the exclude case (original dp) with the include case (dp << num). This effectively parallelizes the DP updates using bitwise operations. The final check (dp & (1 << target)) != 0 tests if bit target is set. While conceptually elegant, this is mainly useful for competitive programming where bitwise operations are highly optimized and when target is not too large.

followups.question: How would you modify the solution to return the actual partition subsets, not just whether partitioning is possible?
followups.hint: Track parent pointers or maintain the path during DP. Backtrack from dp[target] = True to reconstruct which elements were included.

followups.question: What if you needed to partition into k equal subsets instead of 2?
followups.hint: This is problem 698. Use backtracking with k buckets, trying to fill each bucket to target/k. Much more complex than the 2-partition case.

followups.question: How would you handle the case where elements can be negative?
followups.hint: Use offset indexing in DP to handle negative sums. The problem becomes finding if any subset sums to (total-negative_sum)/2.
